headline: A rough day across the board — PLS cratered 8.6%, MSFT dropped 3.4% last night, and Middle East tensions are driving oil higher as a third US carrier arrives in the region.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara got smashed today, falling 8.65% to close at $2.64. Lithium sector uncertainty continues to weigh heavily — news around sector peers like Standard Lithium flagged ongoing market pressure and a cloudy outlook for lithium prices. PLS is now down over 60% from your entry point.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped 3.4% in last night's US session, closing at US$500.39. No single major catalyst, but tech broadly sold off — the NASDAQ fell 1.26%. There's also chatter in markets about hedge fund manager Michael Burry placing bets against the Nasdaq, which rattled sentiment around big tech names.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two fell 4.21% last night to US$204.49, giving back some of its recent GTA 6 hype gains. GTA 6 pre-orders are reportedly near 15 million copies — that's a genuinely massive number — but the stock dipped anyway as the broader tech sell-off dragged it down. The long-term GTA 6 story hasn't changed.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI slipped 1.78% today as uncertainty around the near-term AI outlook weighed on markets globally — Tokyo stocks also extended losses on similar AI concerns. The ETF is now down 18% from your entry.

movers.name: BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF
movers.note: DHHF dropped 1.46% today alongside the broader ASX sell-off (the ASX 200 fell 1.79%). As a diversified global shares ETF, it tracks global market moves closely — today's dip reflects the broader red day, not anything specific to the fund.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG fell 1.36% today in line with the ASX's broad decline. As a diversified multi-asset growth fund, this kind of move on a down market day is completely normal. Nothing stock-specific to flag here.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS eased 1.25% today. The fund tracks the entire US share market, so last night's US sell-off (S&P 500 down 1.2%) flowed through into today's ASX price. Still up 4.8% overall from your entry — holding well.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE dipped 1.14% today. Emerging markets are facing a headwind from a softer Aussie dollar and broader global risk-off sentiment. Down 5.26% from your entry — developing markets can be lumpy, but the long-term diversification case is intact.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google slipped 1.01% last night to US$278.42. No major company-specific news — it moved with the broader NASDAQ sell-off. One bullish analyst note suggested that if Nvidia's upcoming earnings show strong AI chip demand, Alphabet could potentially rise 40% by end of 2026 — a reminder the long-term AI story here remains compelling.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals (PLS) — Another brutal day
watch_today.detail: PLS crashed 8.65% today to $2.64 and is now down over 60% from your entry. The lithium market remains deeply uncertain with no clear price recovery in sight. For a long-term holder, the question is whether the thesis still holds — PLS is a real, operating lithium miner and prices will eventually recover, but this could take years. If you have conviction in lithium's EV future, hold. If this position size is causing you stress, it may be worth reassessing your allocation — but selling at a 60% loss locks in that loss permanently.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Big drop last night, but long-term case unchanged
watch_today.detail: Microsoft fell 3.4% last night to US$500.39 — a chunky single-session move. There's no structural bad news here: Azure cloud and Copilot AI products are still growing. The drop looks like broader tech sentiment and macro jitters rather than anything company-specific. You're still up 12.9% overall. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA 6 pre-orders hit ~15 million, stock still soft
watch_today.detail: Take-Two fell 4.2% last night despite GTA 6 pre-orders reportedly approaching 15 million copies — a genuinely huge number that bodes well for the eventual launch. The dip is about broader market sentiment, not the GTA 6 story. For a long-term holder, this remains a GTA 6 launch play. Hold and let the game do the work.

watch_today.title: RBA minutes released — rate hike debate heating up
watch_today.detail: The RBA's November meeting minutes revealed a split vote on whether to hike rates again. Those who voted against warned of a 'materially sharper economic downturn' if rates go higher. CommBank now says a pause at the next meeting is increasingly likely. This matters for your ASX holdings — a pause would be good news for Australian stocks and property. Watch the RBA's next meeting closely.

watch_today.title: Middle East tensions pushing oil higher — watch inflation
watch_today.detail: A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, Iran is escalating threats, and a tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil (WTI) rose 0.92% last night to US$86.51. If oil keeps rising, it feeds back into inflation — which could force central banks including the RBA to keep rates higher for longer. Worth watching over the coming week.

watch_today.title: GXAI — AI ETF down 18% from entry, but sector still growing
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF is down 18% from what you paid. Today's 1.78% dip adds to that. However, the broader generative AI market is projected to grow massively — one report puts it at US$1.2 trillion by 2035. Short-term noise around AI regulation and outlook is creating volatility, but the long-term direction of AI adoption isn't in doubt. Hold.

world.summary: Middle East tensions are escalating sharply as a third US aircraft carrier arrives in the region, Iran threatens retaliation, and the Houthis seize a key shipping chokepoint. Major US banks are also experiencing outages today.

stories.title: Third US aircraft carrier deployed to Middle East as Iran escalates threats
stories.why_it_matters: The US has now sent a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, bringing thousands more troops to the region. At the same time, Iran is escalating its rhetoric and a commercial tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's most critical shipping lanes through which about 20% of global oil flows. The Houthis (Iran-backed forces in Yemen) have also seized full control of Bab el-Mandeb, another key chokepoint. If shipping through these waterways is disrupted, oil prices spike and global supply chains take a hit — both bad news for inflation and economic stability worldwide.

stories.title: Houthis take full control of Bab el-Mandeb strait after pro-Saudi forces withdraw
stories.why_it_matters: The Houthis now control Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow strait between Yemen and East Africa through which ships must pass to reach the Suez Canal from the Indian Ocean. Pro-Saudi forces have pulled back. This is a major strategic development — the Houthis can now more easily target ships using this route, forcing vessels to take the much longer journey around southern Africa, adding weeks and significant cost to global shipping. It compounds the pressure on oil markets and global supply chains already under strain from the broader Middle East conflict.

stories.title: JPMorgan Chase and other major US banks hit by outages
stories.why_it_matters: JPMorgan Chase and several other major US banks began experiencing outages today. At this stage the cause hasn't been confirmed — it could be a technical failure or something more serious. For everyday people, outages at banks of this size can disrupt payments, transfers and account access. For markets, any suggestion of a cyber attack on financial infrastructure tends to rattle confidence quickly. Worth monitoring as more details emerge.

stories.title: Global economy forecast to grow 2.8% in 2027, but on shaky foundations
stories.why_it_matters: The Swiss Re Institute (a major global insurer and economic research body) is forecasting 2.8% global economic growth in 2027, but warns the foundations are narrow — meaning growth is concentrated in a few sectors and regions, making it fragile. With Middle East conflict, US-China tensions, and persistent inflation still in play, a shock could derail that outlook. For investors, it's a reminder that the global backdrop remains genuinely uncertain even if headline numbers look okay.

stories.title: Robert Pattinson cast as the next James Bond — breaking the franchise's unwritten rule
stories.why_it_matters: Robert Pattinson has reportedly been cast as the next James Bond, reportedly breaking the franchise's longstanding unwritten rule — which has traditionally required a certain look or background for the role. Pattinson, best known for Twilight and The Batman, is a divisive choice that's already generating significant buzz. No financial angle here — just a big pop culture story that'll dominate conversations for a while.

markets.summary: Everything sold off last night and today. The ASX 200 dropped 1.79% to close at 8,883. Last night in the US, the S&P 500 fell 1.2% and the NASDAQ lost 1.26%. Oil is ticking up on Middle East tensions, gold is nudging higher, and the Aussie dollar slipped slightly to 67.4 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Broad selloff today — every sector under pressure. Follows last night's US weakness.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw a risk-off move across US stocks. No single catalyst — a mix of Middle East jitters, rising oil, and tech weakness.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech stocks led the broader pullback last night. MSFT, GOOG and TTWO all slipped.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil rising on Middle East tension — a third US carrier in the region and a tanker struck in the Strait of Hormuz are lifting prices.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold nudging higher as investors seek safety amid geopolitical uncertainty. At near-record levels.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped slightly. A weaker AUD makes your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) worth more in AUD terms when converted.

politics.summary: A big day in Canberra — the RBA's split rate decision is dominating headlines, Treasurer Chalmers is flagging budget cuts in the mid-year update, and the government has reversed course on backpacker work rules.

stories.title: RBA minutes show board was split on latest rate hike — pause increasingly likely next time
stories.why_it_matters: The RBA's November meeting minutes show the board voted to hike rates for a fifth time, but it was a contested decision. The dissenters warned that going too far risked a 'materially sharper economic downturn' — in plain English, they were worried about tipping the economy into a serious recession. CommBank now says a pause at the next meeting is increasingly likely. For everyday Australians with mortgages, this is meaningful: if the RBA pauses, your repayments stop rising. For the share market, a pause is generally a positive signal.

stories.title: Chalmers flags spending cuts in mid-year budget update — 'but not too much'
stories.why_it_matters: Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the upcoming Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook (MYEFO — the mid-year budget update) will include spending cuts, but he's trying to walk a fine line: cut enough to show fiscal responsibility without crushing an economy that's already under pressure from rate hikes. He described it as 'cut enough, but not too much.' With inflation still elevated, the government is under pressure from the RBA to reduce its own spending to help bring prices down.

stories.title: Government reverses backpacker regional work policy
stories.why_it_matters: The Albanese government has backflipped on its policy that required backpackers to spend time working in regional Australia to qualify for a second or third year visa. The government had previously tightened these rules, but is now relaxing them again — likely responding to pressure from agricultural and hospitality industries in regional areas that rely heavily on backpacker labour. For farmers and regional businesses struggling to find workers, this is welcome news.

stories.title: Albanese signs on to Trump's AI supply chain pact at Quad summit
stories.why_it_matters: Prime Minister Albanese has signed Australia on to a US-led AI supply chain agreement at the Quad summit (a grouping of Australia, USA, India and Japan). The deal is about ensuring democratic allies — not China — dominate the global AI hardware and software supply chain. It aligns Australia more closely with the US on technology strategy, which has implications for trade, defence and investment. It also brings Australia into a framework that could shape where AI chips and data centres are built.

stories.title: Paul Kelly calls on Albanese to protect artists' copyright from AI
stories.why_it_matters: Iconic Australian musician Paul Kelly has publicly urged PM Albanese to 'show some backbone' and introduce copyright protections for artists whose work is being used to train AI models without payment or permission. A coalition of Australian creatives — musicians, writers, visual artists — is campaigning for the government to act. The government is currently consulting on AI policy but hasn't committed to specific copyright rules. For anyone who creates content, music, or art professionally, this is a live and significant issue.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the dominant theme today — Australia is moving toward mandatory safety rules, the UN is debating oversight frameworks, and a new Stanford-founded startup has launched with $110 million to let companies build and own their own AI.

stories.title: Australia to impose mandatory safety rules on AI — but are we targeting the right risks?
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian government is moving to introduce mandatory safety rules for AI systems — a world-first approach that goes beyond the voluntary frameworks most other countries are using. The debate now is whether the rules will target the right risks: critics argue the focus is on speculative long-term harms (like AI going rogue) rather than immediate, concrete harms like algorithmic bias in hiring or automated decision-making in welfare and criminal justice. For everyday Australians, mandatory rules mean companies will be legally accountable for how their AI systems behave.

stories.title: New Stanford AI startup Noeri launches with $110M to let companies own their AI
stories.why_it_matters: Noeri, founded by leading AI professors from Stanford University, has launched with $110 million in funding. Its pitch: rather than making companies dependent on OpenAI, Google, or Anthropic, Noeri helps businesses build and actually own their AI systems. This matters because most companies using AI right now are essentially renting it — if the provider changes pricing or terms, they're stuck. Owning your own AI means more control, better privacy for your data, and no vendor lock-in. It's a startup worth watching as the AI industry matures.

stories.title: Generative AI market headed for US$1.2 trillion by 2035 — OpenAI, Microsoft, Google leading the charge
stories.why_it_matters: A new market research report projects the generative AI industry — the technology behind ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini — will be worth US$1.2 trillion by 2035. OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google and Nvidia are identified as the dominant players, all raising record capital and scaling revenue fast. For investors with exposure to GOOG, MSFT, or AI-focused ETFs like GXAI, this is the long-term tailwind underpinning those holdings — even when short-term prices dip.

stories.title: Partly's Interpreter 3 beats Google, OpenAI and Anthropic on automotive repair tasks
stories.why_it_matters: A startup called Partly has released 'Interpreter 3,' a specialised AI model for the automotive repair and parts industry — and it's reportedly outperforming general-purpose AI from Google, OpenAI and Anthropic across all automotive repair tasks. This is a good example of a broader trend: purpose-built AI models trained on specific industry data are beating the giant general models in their own niches. For workshops and mechanics, this kind of AI can accurately identify parts, suggest repairs, and reduce costly errors — practical benefits that are showing up now, not in a distant future.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — the Roosters edged the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. The AFL draft is dominating footy news, with the Magpies, Crows and Eagles all in action. And Jannik Sinner is planning his 2027 tennis comeback.

stories.title: ROOSTERS WIN THE 2026 NRL GRAND FINAL — Beat Knights 19-18 in a one-point classic
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have won the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 at Accor Stadium on Sunday evening. It was an absolute nail-biter — a one-point margin in a Grand Final is as tight as it gets. The Knights had every chance to win it, but the Roosters held on. It's a premiership for the red, white and blue.

stories.title: NRL 2027 pre-season power rankings out — injuries, transfers and scandals shake up the ladder
stories.why_it_matters: With the Grand Final done and dusted, the focus immediately shifts to 2027. Pre-season power rankings are out, factoring in the off-season's injuries, transfers and off-field dramas. No article text available to pull specific rankings, but it's the first look at which clubs are ahead or behind in their pre-season preparation.

stories.title: AFL Draft: Collingwood restore jersey No. 42 for top pick — Crows in talks for major trade
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL draft pre-season is heating up. Collingwood have reinstated jersey No. 42 — the number worn by the late Cam Millane — for their top draft pick, a touching tribute. Meanwhile, the Adelaide Crows are reportedly in talks with a Victorian club to trade for a major draft pick, suggesting they're looking to accelerate their rebuild. Five top picks are also set to be traded, making this one of the more active pre-draft periods in recent years.

stories.title: Jannik Sinner plotting 'brilliant' 2027 tennis return
stories.why_it_matters: World No. 1 Jannik Sinner is reportedly making what's being described as a 'brilliant' strategic move as he plans his return to the ATP Tour in 2027. No specific details from the article text, but Sinner has had a disrupted season and his return strategy is being watched closely by the tennis world. For Australian Open fans, Sinner is always one of the main drawcards — his fitness and form heading into January will be a big storyline.
